Let $M$ be an oriented smooth manifold of finite dimension $n$, possibly with boundary, and set the integration cycle to be $\Gamma=M$ with its given orientation. Let $\mu$ be a smooth positive $n$-form on $M$. The parity-reversed tangent bundle $\Pi TM$ has even base coordinates $x^1,\ldots,x^n$ and odd fiber coordinates $\theta^1,\ldots,\theta^n$ that transform as the coordinate one-forms $dx^i$. Its smooth complex-valued functions are identified with the inhomogeneous complex differential forms $\mathcal A=\Omega^\bullet(M;\mathbb C)$; a form has parity equal to its degree modulo two. Use the Berezin convention $\int d\theta^n\cdots d\theta^1\,\theta^1\cdots\theta^n=1$. For each $F\in\mathcal A$, its degree-$n$ component has a unique expression $F_{[n]}=f_F\mu$ with $f_F\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb C)$. If $f_F\in L^1(M,\mu)$, define

$$I_\Gamma(F):=\int_M f_F\,d\mu=\int_M F_{[n]},$$

where the complex integral is taken componentwise. This is equivalently Berezin integration over the odd fibers followed by integration over the oriented body $M$.

A supercharge $Q$ is a smooth odd derivation of $\mathcal A$: for homogeneous forms $\alpha,\beta$, it satisfies $Q(\alpha\wedge\beta)=Q\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^{|\alpha|}\alpha\wedge Q\beta$. Its square $Q^2:=Q\circ Q$ is an even derivation. The canonical Berezinian density on $\Pi TM$ has local expression $\boldsymbol\mu_\Pi=dx^1\cdots dx^n\,d\theta^n\cdots d\theta^1$ in oriented coordinates. Define divergence relative to this density by

$$\mathcal L_Q\boldsymbol\mu_\Pi=(\operatorname{div}_{\boldsymbol\mu_\Pi}Q)\boldsymbol\mu_\Pi.$$

The condition $\operatorname{div}_{\boldsymbol\mu_\Pi}Q=0$ is local: it says that $Q$ preserves this density. It does not impose any boundary condition. Choose a fixed class $\mathscr C\subseteq\mathcal A$ as part of the integration data. For every $F\in\mathscr C$, require the coefficients of $F_{[n]}$, $(QF)_{[n]}$, and $((\operatorname{div}_{\boldsymbol\mu_\Pi}Q)F)_{[n]}$, relative to $\mu$, to be integrable. Also require a specified finite complex-linear functional $\Phi_{\partial\Gamma}(Q,\cdot)$ on $\mathscr C$, the signed boundary or decay-at-infinity contribution, such that the chosen integration-by-parts identity is

$$I_\Gamma(QF)=\Phi_{\partial\Gamma}(Q,F)-I_\Gamma\bigl((\operatorname{div}_{\boldsymbol\mu_\Pi}Q)F\bigr).$$

This identity is an additional hypothesis on the integration data; its validity must be established from a fully stated integration-by-parts result with its hypotheses checked, or by a direct calculation. No boundary formula for arbitrary manifolds with boundary or noncompact manifolds is asserted here. For $F\in\mathscr C$, call $\Phi_{\partial\Gamma}(Q,F)$ the $Q$-boundary flux of $F$. The integration is $Q$-invariant on $\mathscr C$ when the integrated identity

$$I_\Gamma(QF)=0\qquad\text{for every }F\in\mathscr C$$

holds. The displayed integration-by-parts identity implies that zero divergence and, separately, zero $Q$-boundary flux give the integrated $Q$-invariance identity. Zero divergence alone does not imply it. For a compact manifold without boundary the boundary contribution is absent in the usual compact-supermanifold formula; on a noncompact manifold or one with boundary, vanishing flux must be established from the chosen decay and boundary conditions.

An admissible finite-dimensional $Q$-exact deformation consists of even smooth forms $S,O\in\mathcal A$, an odd smooth form $V\in\mathcal A$, and a nonempty open interval $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ such that the integration is $Q$-invariant on $\mathscr C$ and $QS=QO=0$. The even form $QV$ is the $Q$-exact deformation, $S_t:=S+tQV$, and $E_t:=e^{-S_t}$, where the exponential is the pointwise exponential of the degree-zero part times the finite exterior-degree expansion of its positive-degree part. Require $(Q^2V)E_t=0$ for every $t\in J$; the stronger condition $Q^2V=0$ is sufficient. Require $O E_t$ and $O V E_t$ to belong to $\mathscr C$ for every $t\in J$, so $I_\Gamma(Q(O V E_t))=0$. If this identity is established by graded integration by parts, its zero-divergence and zero-boundary-flux hypotheses are separate.

Write $(O E_t)_{[n]}=f_t\mu$. The deformation data are analytically admissible when $f_t\in L^1(M,\mu)$ for every $t\in J$, and for $\mu$-almost every $x$ the map $t\mapsto f_t(x)$ is differentiable at every $t\in J$ as a map from a real interval to $\mathbb C$, with

$$\partial_t f_t(x):=\lim_{\substack{h\to0\\ h\in\mathbb R,\ h\ne0,\ t+h\in J}}\frac{f_{t+h}(x)-f_t(x)}{h}\in\mathbb C.$$

For each $t$, require $x\mapsto\partial_t f_t(x)$ to be measurable, using zero on the common exceptional null set. For every compact $K\subset J$, require a single nonnegative $g_K\in L^1(M,\mu)$ that bounds both $|f_t(x)|$ and $|\partial_t f_t(x)|$ for every $t\in K$ outside one $\mu$-null set. The underlying manifold is finite-dimensional; its smooth-function algebra need not be finite-dimensional as a vector space.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval and let $f:X\times I\to\mathbb C$
be such that:

1. for every $t\in I$, the function $x\mapsto f(x,t)$ is integrable;
2. for almost every $x$, the map $t\mapsto f(x,t)$ is differentiable on $I$;
3. for every $t\in I$, the function
   $$x\mapsto \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t),$$
   extended by zero where the derivative is undefined, is measurable;
4. there are a measurable null set $N$ and a nonnegative measurable function
   $g$ with
   $$\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$$
   and
   $$\left|\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\right|\le g(x)$$
   for every $t\in I$ and every $x\in X\setminus N$.

Then
$$F(t):=\int f(x,t)\,d\mu(x)$$
is differentiable on $I$, and
$$F'(t)=\int \frac{\partial f}{\partial t}(x,t)\,d\mu(x),$$
with the same zero extension in the last integral.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
(Complete ordered field (least-upper-bound property)), neighbourhoods are those of
The $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood and the punctured $\varepsilon$-neighbourhood of a point of $\mathbb{R}$ and limit points those of Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$ defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by At a limit point of the domain a function has at most one limit applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$ leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
(The $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ limit $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = L$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a limit point $c$ of $A$). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of The limit at $c$ depends only on the restriction of $f$ to a punctured neighbourhood of $c$, and passes to any subset of the domain having $c$ as a limit point carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
(Limit point, isolated point, adherent point, derived set, and dense subset of $\mathbb{R}$).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex (Intervals of $\mathbb{R}$: the nine order-convex forms, nondegeneracy, and length) and let
$f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ (Continuity of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point of $A$ and on $A$: the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, its agreement with $\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)$ at a limit point, and continuity at an isolated point) and
differentiable at every point of $I$ that is interior to $I$
(Interior, closure, boundary and exterior of a subset of $\mathbb{R}$, The derivative $f'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}$ of $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ at a point $c \in A$ that is a limit point of $A$, and differentiability on a set), with

$$f'(x) = 0 \qquad \text{at every interior point } x \text{ of } I .$$

Then $f$ is constant on $I$: there is a real $k$ with $f(x) = k$ for every
$x \in I$.

Consequently, if $f, g : I \to \mathbb{R}$ are both continuous on $I$ and both
differentiable at every interior point of $I$, with $f'(x) = g'(x)$ at every
interior point $x$, then there is a real $k$ with

$$f(x) \;=\; g(x) + k \qquad \text{for every } x \in I .$$

**Order-convexity of $I$ is essential and is not a convenience.** The
conclusion is false on a domain that falls into separate pieces, since a
function may be constant on each piece with different constants; nothing in the
proof would survive, because the mean value theorem is applied to the segment
joining two points of the domain and that segment must lie in the domain.

**The hypothesis is imposed only at interior points.** At an endpoint of $I$
nothing is asked at all: $f$ need not be differentiable there, and the proof
never evaluates a difference quotient at an endpoint, since it applies the mean
value theorem on a segment $[u,v] \subseteq I$ and uses the derivative only at
points of $(u,v)$, all of which are interior to $I$. What is *not* meant is that
the derivative at an endpoint is free to be nonzero: once $f$ is known to be
constant its difference quotient at an endpoint is constantly $0$, so wherever
$f'$ exists at an endpoint it is $0$ too. That is a consequence of the theorem,
not a hypothesis of it.

derivations.claim: Put $E_t=e^{-S-tQV}$. Since $QV$ is even, coefficientwise differentiation of its exponential gives $\partial_tE_t=-(QV)E_t$. The top-degree projection is linear and $O$ is independent of $t$, so $(\partial_t f_t)\mu=-[O(QV)E_t]_{[n]}$.
The assumptions $QS=0$ and $(Q^2V)E_t=0$ give $QE_t=-(QS+tQ^2V)E_t=0$. The graded Leibniz rule, $QO=0$, and the odd parity of $V$ then give $Q(OV E_t)=(QO)VE_t+O(QV)E_t-OV(QE_t)=O(QV)E_t$.

Fix $t_0\in J$ and choose $a<t_0<b$ with $[a,b]\subset J$. The majorant $g_{[a,b]}$ makes every $f_t$ integrable on $(a,b)$ and bounds its measurable parameter derivative there by one $L^1(M,\mu)$ function. Applying [F2] on $(a,b)$, and using step 1.1, gives $Z'(t_0)=-I_\Gamma(O(QV)E_{t_0})$.

Substituting step 1.2 into the derivative formula of step 2.1 yields $Z'(t_0)=-I_\Gamma(Q(OV E_{t_0}))=0$ by the exact integrated $Q$-invariance identity assumed in the Statement for $F=OV E_{t_0}$. Since $t_0$ was arbitrary, $Z'$ vanishes throughout $J$.

Write $Z=u+iv$ with real functions $u,v$. Step 3.1 implies that both real difference quotients have limit zero at every $t\in J$. By [F3], for each $t$ and all sufficiently small nonzero $h$, $|u(t+h)-u(t)|<|h|$ and $|v(t+h)-v(t)|<|h|$; hence $u$ and $v$ are continuous at every $t$. Applying [F4] to each component shows that both are constant on $J$. Therefore $Z$ is constant on $J$.

derivations.claim: For a smooth periodic three-form $\eta=\sum_{i=1}^4(-1)^{i-1}a_i(x)\,dx^1\wedge\cdots\widehat{dx^i}\cdots\wedge dx^4$, the degree-four coefficient of $d\eta$ is $\sum_i\partial_i a_i$. For each $i$, integrating $\partial_i a_i$ over $x^i\in[0,2\pi]$ gives $a_i|_{x^i=2\pi}-a_i|_{x^i=0}=0$ by periodicity; iterated integration over the other three coordinates therefore gives $\int_{T^4}(d\eta)_{[4]}=0$. Thus $I_\Gamma(QF)=0$ for every $F$.

Directly, $QO=QS=0$, $QV=dV=\cos(x^3)\,dx^3\wedge dx^4$, and $Q^2V=d(dV)=-\sin(x^3)\,dx^3\wedge dx^3\wedge dx^4=0$. For $t$ in any compact interval $K$, the coefficients of $Oe^{-S-tQV}$ and its $t$-derivative are bounded on the compact torus by $1+\sup_{t\in K}|t|$; this constant is integrable on $T^4$. Therefore [F2] applies.
